Latchkey Kid
LATCH-kee kid
noun (Gen X slang)
From latchkey, the key that lifts the latch of an outer door (19th century). Latchkey children was in American use by the 1940s for the children of wartime working mothers, who wore the house key on a string around the neck. The phrase returned in force in the 1970s and 1980s, when rising divorce and two-income households left millions of Gen X children to let themselves in after school; after-school specials and safety pamphlets on answering the door and the phone followed. It is the defining childhood image of the generation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A latchkey kid was a child who came home from school to an empty house, the key on a shoelace around his neck. He let himself in, made a snack, and waited for a parent to come home from work. For a large part of Gen X this was simply childhood: divorce had climbed, both parents often worked, and the 3 p.m. house was quiet. Many of those children learned real independence and resourcefulness. Many also learned loneliness early. The Christian observation begins with compassion, not blame. Most parents of that era were doing their best in hard circumstances, and many a single mother wore herself out providing. But Scripture is honest that God designed children to be raised in the company of their parents: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way" (Deu 6:7). The promise of the gospel includes turning "the heart of the fathers to the children" (Mal 4:6). And for every child who sat alone, God reveals Himself in a particular way: "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation" (Psa 68:5); "God setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6). "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up" (Psa 27:10). Christ promised, "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you" (Joh 14:18). A Gen X father who was a latchkey kid can tell his son plainly: I remember the empty house; God was in it, though I did not know it; and I want our home to be one where you are not alone. Where he cannot always be home, the church can be the family into which God sets the solitary.

Webster 1828 Definition

A child who lets himself into an empty house after school (US, 1940s; the defining Gen X childhood of the 1970s–80s); Scripture meets that child with a Father of the fatherless who setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:5-6).

expand to see more

LATCHKEY KID, n. (Gen X slang, US, from the 1940s; widespread 1970s–80s) A child who returns from school to an empty home and lets himself in, the parents being at work. "I was a latchkey kid — key on a shoelace, TV on till Mom got home."

Also latchkey child; from the house key worn on a string or shoelace around the neck.

1980s companions: the after-school special, safety pamphlets on answering the phone and the door, the microwave snack.

Webster 1828: LATCH, n. [Latin ligula, from ligo, to tie, and with English lock. Latin laqueus, from which we have lace, may belong to the same root. The primary sense of the root is to catch, to close, stop or make fast.] 1. A small piece of iron or wood used to fasten a door. …

Decode for parents: many Gen X fathers and mothers were latchkey kids; remember the empty house with compassion, and build a home where your children are not alone.

Key Scripture

Psa 68:5 — "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation."

Psa 68:6 — "God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land."

Psa 27:10 — "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up."

Deu 6:7 — "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Joh 14:18 — "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you."

Modern Corruption

The latchkey childhood was usually no one’s cruelty but a culture’s drift away from the home; Scripture answers with a God who is Father of the fatherless and sets the solitary in families.

expand to see more

A culture’s drift, not a villain. It would be easy and unjust to blame the parents. Many were widowed, divorced, or unable to pay the mortgage on one income, and they worked hard for children they loved. The deeper cause was a culture that came to treat the home as a place to sleep between jobs and school. Deuteronomy pictures something else: parents and children together in the house and by the way, the Word passing between them in ordinary hours (Deu 6:7). Children cannot be taught diligently by an empty kitchen.

God in the empty house. The good news for every grown latchkey kid is that he was never as alone as he felt. God is "a father of the fatherless" (Psa 68:5) and the One who "setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6). When father and mother are absent, "the LORD will take me up" (Psa 27:10). Christ refuses to leave His people comfortless (Joh 14:18). The church is meant to be part of that answer: older saints, open homes, and a table where any child who would otherwise be alone at three o’clock is welcome.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English læccan (to seize) → latch, latchkey → US latchkey children (1940s) → the Gen X after-school childhood (1970s–80s); Scripture: God setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:6).

expand to see more

Old English læccan — to seize, to grasp; latch, a door fastening

19th c.: latchkey — the key that lifts the outer latch

1940s US: latchkey children of wartime working mothers

1970s–80s: divorce and two-income homes make it the defining Gen X childhood

Biblical answer: a father of the fatherless (Psa 68:5); I will not leave you comfortless (Joh 14:18)
